## `Kotton`

Kotton - Your data sovereignty platform

**Usage:** `Kotton [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `login` — Authenticate and cache a session token for a user
* `app` — App lifecycle (list, launch, new, sideload, build, rm, …) — shares the REPL's `app` verb
* `id` — Identity management — your identities on this device (list, use, create, recover, rotate, unlock)
* `whoami` — Show the identity your commands act as (the active identity)
* `repl` — Launch the interactive REPL for a user
* `peer` — Peer node management (identity, list, show, add, revoke, mount) — shares the REPL's `peer` verb
* `device` — Manage the devices on your identity — add, join, list, revoke, name (six-digit pairing) — shares the REPL's `device` verb. `reset` is the exception: it starts this whole device fresh and needs no daemon
* `schema` — Schema management (list, show, register)
* `handler` — Handler registry (register, unregister, get, list, set-default)
* `record` — Record addressing — open records by kotton:// URL
* `records` — The project's records in a root its org owns — init, invite, import, export
* `import` — Bring your history with you — read an export (.ics) into your own records
* `sync` — Sync this device's drives, now — the REPL's `sync`, one parser for both
* `drive` — Your drives — create, list, show, move, enrol — the REPL's `drive`, one parser for both
* `pin` — What this device keeps of your drives — default, a drive or folder, list — the REPL's `pin`, one parser for both
* `status` — When this device last synced, what it keeps of each drive, and the notices — shares the REPL's `status` verb
* `issuer` — Trusted-issuer registry (add, remove, list) — shares the REPL's `issuer` verb
* `cp` — Copy files into and out of your tree — shares the REPL's `cp` verb. `host:` names this computer's own files, a relative one from the directory the command is run in
* `keep` — Keep a folder of yours in your tree, and copy only what changed when run again — shares the REPL's `keep` verb. The folder is on this computer, a relative one from the directory the command is run in; with no arguments it lists what is kept
* `cat` — Print a file in your tree — shares the REPL's `cat` verb
* `mint` — Make the key a relay or a vault of your own is created for, and print the command its host runs — shares the REPL's `mint` verb
* `enrol` — Complete a key `mint` made, from the line its relay or vault printed when it was created — shares the REPL's `enrol` verb
* `relay` — This device's relay (set, clear, status), and a relay of your own (rule, invite, forget) — shares the REPL's `relay` verb
* `vault` — A vault of your own (people, invite, digits, space, drop, stand, move, forget) — shares the REPL's `vault` verb
* `grant` — Grant management (revoke, import)
* `extension` — Confined extensions (install, list, remove)
* `contact` — The people you can message — pair, join, list
* `message` — Messaging (send, inbox, channels)
* `org` — Org identity management (new, show, list, grant, member)
* `config` — Device configuration — relay, TURN, STUN
* `model` — The models you have installed — add, ls, rm, use
* `net` — Network status snapshot (peers, gateways, sync, rendezvous)

###### **Options:**

* `--json` — Machine-readable output: print shapes as JSON instead of styled text. Put it before the verb (`kotton --json issuer list`). Only the shared verbs that emit shapes honor it. A verb that reads `--json` among its own words (`drive`, `pin`) is handed the word instead, so `kotton --json drive list` is `kotton drive list --json`, as the REPL's `drive list --json` is. There it is for `list` and `show` alone, and any other verb refuses it, exit 2 (`kotton --json drive create …`, `kotton --json pin <drive> whole`)

## `Kotton app`

App lifecycle (list, launch, new, sideload, build, rm, …) — shares the REPL's `app` verb

**Usage:** `Kotton app [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
app — manage installed apps

USAGE:
  app list                      list all installed apps
  app new <name>                scaffold an app: a manifest and one wasm32-wasip2 crate
  app sideload <path>           show what a WASM app asks for, then --approve it
  app grants <id>               what an installed app asked for, and what it holds
  app launch <id> [key=value …] launch an installed app with optional args
  app install <path>            install a web bundle (production)
  app dev <path>                register a live dev bundle (shows '(dev)' in list)
  app rm <id>                   remove an installed app
  app build <path>              build logic/ (cargo component) and ui/ (pnpm build)
  app set-role <role> <id>      assign a named system role to an app id
  app verify <id>               re-hash the WASM binary and check integrity

<path> can be the app source directory (e.g. ./apps/kotton-shell) or its
dist/ subdirectory.  The app id is read from manifest.toml automatically.

EXAMPLES:
  app new my-app
  app sideload ./apps/kotton-shell
  app sideload ./apps/kotton-shell --approve
  app grants sh.kotton.shell
  app launch sh.kotton.shell
  app build ./apps/kotton-shell
  app set-role shell sh.kotton.shell
  app list
  app rm sh.kotton.shell
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments to the verb: `list` | `launch <id>` | `new <name>` | `sideload <path>` | `rm <id>` | …

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton id`

Identity management — your identities on this device (list, use, create, recover, rotate, unlock)

**Usage:** `Kotton id <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `create` — Create a new identity on this device. Prompts for a name if omitted
* `join` — Join an identity you have on another device: run `kotton device add` there, then this here
* `rm` — Remove a user from this device
* `add-recovery` — Set up recovery: mint a 24-word phrase and commit it as an authority
* `login` — Recover an account with a 24-word recovery phrase (prompted, hidden)
* `rotate` — Rotate your identity key with your recovery phrase (survive key compromise). Your identity (DID) stays the same; the old key stops working. The phrase is prompted (hidden), never taken on the command line
* `recover` — Make this machine yours again, from the words and the line `id add-recovery` printed. Asks for your name (unless given), the twenty-four words at a hidden prompt, the vault's line, and a passphrase for this machine, before it begins. Then it claims the name here, adds the vault the line names, fetches your identity and sealed keys from it, proves the words against them, makes this machine's key yours, seals your keys here under the passphrase, records the vault as your drive, makes the identity the one this machine acts as, and syncs your things back. Words that do not prove the identity are refused: a machine that held nothing of the name holds nothing of it after, unless the refusal names lines to run, in order, to remove what it could not take back; and one that held it keeps it
* `set-passphrase` — Set your daily unlock passphrase, so you unlock with it — not your recovery phrase
* `bind-device` — Bind this identity to this device's hardware, so the vault opens only here
* `lock` — Lock your vault now — your keys leave memory until your passphrase opens it again
* `unlock` — Unlock this device's session with your daily passphrase
* `list` — List all identities loaded on this device (`*` marks the active one)
* `use` — Set the active identity — the one your commands act as by default



## `Kotton id create`

Create a new identity on this device. Prompts for a name if omitted

**Usage:** `Kotton id create [USERNAME]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<USERNAME>` — Username / identity ID (prompted interactively if omitted)



## `Kotton id join`

Join an identity you have on another device: run `kotton device add` there, then this here.

This device shows six digits; type them where `device add` asks for them, and answer `y` here. It ends with the identity on this device, acting as it when it acted as nobody. Needs no identity on this device first: it is how one arrives. The shell's `device join`, run as `<username>`.

**Usage:** `Kotton id join <USERNAME> [CODE]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<USERNAME>` — What this device calls the identity (it need not match the other device's)
* `<CODE>` — The code `device add` printed; leave it out to find that device on this network

###### **Options:**

## `Kotton id add-recovery`

Set up recovery: mint a 24-word phrase and commit it as an authority.

Prints the twenty-four words and, under them, the line of each vault that keeps a copy of your sealed keys, once: write both on paper. `id recover` asks for them on any machine. Creation mints no phrase, so this is how an identity gains a way back in. It can be run more than once — the committed set only ever grows, so an added phrase never retires one you already have. Named for what it *adds*, not for recovering: `id recover` is the act, and two commands whose names both say "recover" would be one name for the setup and the act.

**Usage:** `Kotton id add-recovery <USERNAME>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<USERNAME>` — Username / identity ID



## `Kotton id login`

Recover an account with a 24-word recovery phrase (prompted, hidden)

**Usage:** `Kotton id login <USERNAME>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<USERNAME>` — Username to restore (required when this is a fresh device)

* `<USERNAME>` — Username / identity ID



## `Kotton id recover`

Make this machine yours again, from the words and the line `id add-recovery` printed. Asks for your name (unless given), the twenty-four words at a hidden prompt, the vault's line, and a passphrase for this machine, before it begins. Then it claims the name here, adds the vault the line names, fetches your identity and sealed keys from it, proves the words against them, makes this machine's key yours, seals your keys here under the passphrase, records the vault as your drive, makes the identity the one this machine acts as, and syncs your things back. Words that do not prove the identity are refused: a machine that held nothing of the name holds nothing of it after, unless the refusal names lines to run, in order, to remove what it could not take back; and one that held it keeps it

**Usage:** `Kotton id recover [USERNAME]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<USERNAME>` — Username / identity ID (asked for if omitted)

Unlock this device's session with your daily passphrase

###### **Options:**

* `--repair` — Repair your keys from your vault while unlocking: a key this device cannot read, or does not hold, is written back from the vault your passphrase opens. A key that reads is checked against the vault and never written over — if one differs, nothing is written and the refusal names it

## `Kotton peer`

Peer node management (identity, list, show, add, revoke, mount) — shares the REPL's `peer` verb

**Usage:** `Kotton peer [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
peer — manage paired peer nodes

USAGE:
  peer identity                                    print this node's DID and signing key
  peer list                                        paired peers: the remote `peer show <remote>` takes,
                                                   where each is reachable, and its relay
  peer show <remote>                               one peer whole: its line (the one `id recover` asks
                                                   for), its full DID, key, and `peer add` line
  peer add <remote> <did> <pubkey-hex> <addr>      add a peer manually (no ceremony)
  peer revoke <remote>                             remove a peer from the allowlist
  peer mount list                                  list configured peer mounts
  peer mount add <node> <remote-path> <local-path> [--budget N] [--pin p]
                                                   mount a path from a peer
  peer mount evict <node> <local-path>             evict a mount's local cache
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments to the verb: `list` | `show <remote>` | `add …` | `revoke <remote>` | `mount …`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton device`

Manage the devices on your identity — add, join, list, revoke, name (six-digit pairing) — shares the REPL's `device` verb. `reset` is the exception: it starts this whole device fresh and needs no daemon

**Usage:** `Kotton device [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
device add|join|list|name|revoke — pair another of your machines to this identity (six-digit confirmation); `--browser` admits a phone's browser, `--gateway <code>` a gateway elsewhere. A vault's invite is `drive enrol <invite>`. `kotton device reset` starts this whole device fresh and is the CLI's, not this shell's — it deletes the directory this runtime is using

RETIRED:
  device admit             gone: type `drive enrol`
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments to the verb: `add [--as NAME] [--blind|--cosigner]` | `add --browser` | `add --gateway <code>` | `join [code] [--as NAME]` | `list` | `revoke <id>` | `revoke --browser <name>` | `name [NAME]` | `reset [--yes]`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)

## `Kotton record open`

Open a record by its kotton:// URL and print its JSON body.

Example: kotton record open kotton://records/sh.kotton.notes/019612ab-e3f2-7000-abcd-1234567890ab

**Usage:** `Kotton record open --user <USER> <URL>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<URL>` — The full `kotton://records/<nsid>/<id>` URL

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity that owns the record (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton records`

The project's records in a root its org owns — init, invite, import, export

**Usage:** `Kotton records <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `init` — Create the project's root under an org's identity, with you as its first member and `org.invite` on it delegated to you; register the record schema; and grant the converter read and write on it
* `invite` — Let someone into the project's root, under the `org.invite` you hold on it. Name them as `kotton contact list` shows them, or by their AID; the AID invited is printed, with their membership grant, for them to hold
* `import` — Read every record file in a directory into the project's root, inserting or replacing each by its name. A second import of the same files changes nothing
* `export` — Write every row of the project's root back to a directory, one file per record



## `Kotton records init`

## `Kotton sync`

Sync this device's drives, now — the REPL's `sync`, one parser for both

**Usage:** `Kotton sync [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
sync — sync this device's drives, now

USAGE:
  sync [--no-wait]

A device syncs to your drives, never to another device: your other devices
get what this one writes by way of a drive. What this device keeps of each
drive is `pin`'s: `pin list` says it.

FLAGS:
  --no-wait   start the sync and return; `status` says when it last synced
  --push, --pull, --node
              gone, exit 2: a device is not a sync target

Exit 0 when done, 1 when refused (the reason on stderr), 2 for a line that is
not the one above.

RETIRED:
  sync now                 is `sync`, and still runs it
  sync add                 gone: type `pin <drive>`
  sync list                gone: type `pin list`
  sync remove              gone: type `pin <drive>`
  sync <remote>            gone: type `sync`
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments: none, or `--no-wait` (the words this verb retired are in the RETIRED block, from its table)

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton drive`

Your drives — create, list, show, move, enrol — the REPL's `drive`, one parser for both

**Usage:** `Kotton drive [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
drive — your drives: where your things live

USAGE:
  drive create <name> [--on <vault>]   make a drive on one of your vaults
  drive list [--json]                  every drive: its id, where it lives, its size, which devices keep it whole
  drive show <name> [--json]           one drive, on each vault it is kept on
  drive move <name> --to <vault> [--from <vault>]
                                       carry a drive, sealed, to another of your vaults
  drive enrol <invite>                 take a vault's invite: the vault keeps drives for you

A drive is a sealed tree a vault keeps for you; a vault keeps as many as you
make. Its name is sealed under your key: the vault cannot read it. Your first
drive on each vault is `personal`, the tree this device syncs with.

A move copies every sealed object to the other vault under the same key, and
retires the drive where it was only once the other vault holds all of it.
Your other devices follow it at their next sync. A move that fails leaves the
drive where it was; a copy the other vault would not take back is listed as an
unfinished move, and moving the drive there again clears it. A move cut off
after the other vault has the drive is finished by running it again. A key the
vault lists that is not a storage key is refused, not carried, and noted in the
move's answer; `logs --level warn`, in the REPL, names it. `personal` does not
move.

`enrol` takes the invite a vault's landlord gave you (`vault invite <name>`
at theirs): this device meets the vault at the invite's relay, and you type
the six digits they read out. The vault keeps sealed what you put on a drive
there and can read none of it. It asks nothing else.

FLAGS:
  --on <vault>   the vault to make the drive on: its label, DID or key
                 (needed when you keep drives on more than one)
  --to <vault>   the vault to move the drive to: its label, DID or key
  --from <vault> the copy to move, where two drives of yours share a name
  --json         `list` and `show`: what the vaults answered, as JSON on stdout

Exit 0 when done, 1 when refused (the reason on stderr), 2 for a line that is
not one of the above.

EXAMPLES:
  drive create photos                  # on your one vault
  drive create work --on office-vault  # on the vault labelled office-vault
  drive list
  drive show photos
  drive move photos --to office-vault
  drive list --json
  drive enrol <invite>                 # the invite the landlord gave you
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments: `create <name> [--on <vault>]` | `list [--json]` | `show <name> [--json]` | `move <name> --to <vault>` | `enrol <invite>`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton pin`

What this device keeps of your drives — default, a drive or folder, list — the REPL's `pin`, one parser for both

**Usage:** `Kotton pin [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
pin — what this device keeps of your drives

USAGE:
  pin default whole|on-demand                       this device's default, for every drive it has not been told about
  pin <drive>[:/<folder>] whole|on-demand|default   set a drive or a folder the other way on this device
  pin list [--json]                                 this device's default and exceptions, and the notices

  whole       keep on this device: every file's content is here, opened or not
  on-demand   fetch when opened: this device keeps the index — every name, and
              where its content is — and fetches a file's content when it is opened
  default     follow the setting above: a folder its drive's, a drive this device's default

Every device of yours sees every drive. The nearest setting wins: a folder's
over its drive's over this device's default. Your first device starts at
whole; a device paired later at on demand. Pins hold for `personal` today: a
device keeps no tree of a drive made with `drive create` yet, so its vault
alone holds it, and `status` says so.

`pin <drive> whole` collects: this device fetches what it lacks of the drive
now. A pinned file brings the pack it was written in: whatever else was written
beside it at the same sync comes with it, and stays while the pin does. Each
setting stays on this device. What your other devices learn is only that this
device keeps a drive whole: one record in that drive per device that does,
sealed like everything else, so the vault cannot read it.

You are told when no device of yours keeps a drive whole, and when this device
runs short of room for what it keeps whole, with the setting that keeps less.

FLAGS:
  --json   `list`: this device's default, exceptions and notices, as JSON on stdout

Exit 0 when done, 1 when refused (the reason on stderr), 2 for a line that is
not one of the above.

EXAMPLES:
  pin default on-demand         # fetch when opened, unless told otherwise
  pin personal:/photos whole    # keep this folder on this device
  pin personal:/photos default
  pin personal whole            # collect all my things
  pin list
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments: `default whole|on-demand` | `<drive>[:/<folder>] whole|on-demand|default` | `list [--json]`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)

###### **Options:**

## `Kotton cp`

Copy files into and out of your tree — shares the REPL's `cp` verb. `host:` names this computer's own files, a relative one from the directory the command is run in

**Usage:** `Kotton cp [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
cp — copy files or directories

USAGE:
  cp <src> <dst>

Paths are VFS paths by default.  Prefix with host: to reference the host
filesystem.

  cp /foo /bar              VFS → VFS
  cp host:./file.txt /bar   host → VFS
  cp /foo host:./file.txt   VFS → host

Directories are copied recursively.

EXAMPLES:
  cp /notes/a.txt /notes/b.txt
  cp host:./config.json /settings/config.json
  cp /exports host:./backup
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments: `<src> <dst>`, each a path in your tree or `host:<path>` on this computer

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton keep`

Keep a folder of yours in your tree, and copy only what changed when run again — shares the REPL's `keep` verb. The folder is on this computer, a relative one from the directory the command is run in; with no arguments it lists what is kept

**Usage:** `Kotton keep [OPTIONS] [ARGS]...`

```text
keep — keep a folder of yours in your tree, and pick up its changes

USAGE:
  keep <folder> [as /<name>]
  keep

Copies every file under <folder>, a folder on this computer, into your
tree at /<name>, sealed on disk as cp seals what it copies. <name> is the
folder's own name unless you give one. A relative <folder> is from the
directory the command is run in, and ~ is your home folder. Each file is
read whole into memory as it is copied, as cp reads it.

Hidden files are copied too. Symbolic links are not followed: each is
skipped and counted in what keep prints.

Run it again to pick up changes. A file whose size and modification time
are what they were when it was last copied, and which is still in your
tree, is left as it is and makes no new version; changed and new files are
copied. A file deleted from the folder stays in your tree, and a change
made in your tree is not copied back to the folder.

What is kept is recorded in your tree, sealed as your files are, at
/.kept/<device>.json, one file for each device. keep on a device reads
and writes that device's record alone; every device's record is a file
of yours, which cp and rm reach as they reach any. A name kept from a folder that is gone from this computer is
taken by the next folder kept under it.

With no arguments, keep lists each folder kept from this device, where in
your tree it is, and whether the folder is gone.

EXAMPLES:
  keep ~/Photos
  keep ~/Documents/taxes as /taxes
  keep
```

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ARGS>` — Arguments: `<folder> [as /<name>]`, a folder on this computer and where in your tree it goes; none lists what is kept

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act as, before the verb's words (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)


## `Kotton grant`

Grant management (revoke, import)

**Usage:** `Kotton grant <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `revoke` — Add an envelope ID to the local revocation list
* `import` — Import a cross-DID `GrantEnvelope` issued by an org



## `Kotton grant revoke`

Add an envelope ID to the local revocation list.

Any IPC calls from apps whose `GrantEnvelope` matches this ID will be denied after this point. Revocation is immediately effective and irreversible on this device.

**Usage:** `Kotton grant revoke --user <USER> <ENVELOPE_ID>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<ENVELOPE_ID>` — The UUID from `GrantEnvelope.id` to revoke

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on



## `Kotton grant import`

Import a cross-DID `GrantEnvelope` issued by an org.

The envelope must be a JSON file. Pass `--stdin` to read from stdin instead of a file path. The daemon verifies the issuer is in the trusted-issuer registry and that the signature is valid before storing.

**Usage:** `Kotton grant import [OPTIONS] --user <USER> [PATH]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<PATH>` — Path to the JSON file containing the `GrantEnvelope`.

   Omit (or use `-`) to read from stdin.

###### **Options:**

* `--stdin` — Read the envelope JSON from stdin instead of a file
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on

## `Kotton message channel admit`

Admit a contact to a channel you hold the key for.

The channel moves to its next key, granted to everyone in it and to them: they read from here on, not what was said before. Name them as `kotton contact list` shows them, or by DID. Somebody you hold no key for is refused, and the refusal is the daemon's, as it said it.

**Usage:** `Kotton message channel admit --user <USER> <CHANNEL_ID> <CONTACT>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<CHANNEL_ID>`
* `<CONTACT>` — A contact's name, as `kotton contact list` shows it, or their DID

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>`



## `Kotton message channel remove`

Remove a member from a channel you hold the key for.

The channel moves to its next key, granted to everyone in it but them: what is said from here on does not open for them. What they were in for stays theirs to read. Name them as `kotton contact list` shows them, or by DID. Yourself, or somebody who is not in the channel, is refused, and the refusal is the daemon's, as it said it.

**Usage:** `Kotton message channel remove --user <USER> <CHANNEL_ID> <CONTACT>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<CHANNEL_ID>`
* `<CONTACT>` — A contact's name, as `kotton contact list` shows it, or their DID

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>`



## `Kotton message channel leave`

Leave a channel: tell its members, then let go of its keys.

Nothing said in it after this opens for you. Files shared with you stay yours; the conversation's text stays in your store and no longer opens, since its keys are gone.

**Usage:** `Kotton message channel leave --user <USER> <CHANNEL_ID>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<CHANNEL_ID>`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>`

Issue a GrantEnvelope from an org DID to a member DID.

Prints the envelope JSON to stdout so you can share it out-of-band.

**Usage:** `Kotton org grant issue [OPTIONS] --org <ORG> --to <TO> --cap <CAPS> --user <USER>`

###### **Options:**

* `--org <ORG>` — The org DID (`did:key:…`) that issues the grant
* `--to <TO>` — The member DID (`did:key:…`) that receives the grant
* `--cap <CAPS>` — Capabilities to grant, e.g. `schema.read:sh.kotton.notes`. Repeat for multiple capabilities
* `--ttl <TTL>` — Optional time-to-live in seconds
* `--node <NODE>` — Optional node DID to restrict scope to a specific node
* `--user <USER>` — User ID who owns the org key



## `Kotton org grant list`

List all grants issued by an org

**Usage:** `Kotton org grant list --org <ORG> --user <USER>`

###### **Options:**

* `--org <ORG>` — The org DID (`did:key:…`)
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on behalf of



## `Kotton org member`

Member management for an org

**Usage:** `Kotton org member <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `remove` — Revoke all grants issued to a member DID and remove them from the org



## `Kotton org member remove`

Revoke all grants issued to a member DID and remove them from the org

**Usage:** `Kotton org member remove --org <ORG> --user <USER> <MEMBER_DID>`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — User ID who owns the org key



## `Kotton org frost`

FROST multi-sig key management and signing ceremonies

**Usage:** `Kotton org frost <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `new` — Create a new FROST multi-sig org (trusted-dealer key generation)
* `join` — Join a FROST org by importing the key share sent by the initiator
* `sign-contribute` — Co-signer: contribute to an in-progress signing ceremony
* `sign-finalize` — Coordinator: finalize the signing ceremony and issue the GrantEnvelope



## `Kotton org frost new`

Create a new FROST multi-sig org (trusted-dealer key generation).

The initiator generates all key shares. Shares for other participants are printed and must be sent to each participant over a secure channel. Each participant imports their share with `kotton org frost join`.

**Usage:** `Kotton org frost new --threshold <THRESHOLD> --total <TOTAL> --user <USER> <NAME>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<NAME>` — Human-readable org name

###### **Options:**

* `--threshold <THRESHOLD>` — Minimum co-signers required for a valid signature (t in t-of-n)
* `--total <TOTAL>` — Total number of participants (n in t-of-n)
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on behalf of



## `Kotton org frost join`

Join a FROST org by importing the key share sent by the initiator

**Usage:** `Kotton org frost join --org-did <ORG_DID> --share <SHARE> --index <INDEX> --user <USER> <NAME>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<NAME>` — Human-readable org name (used locally for display)

###### **Options:**

* `--org-did <ORG_DID>` — Org DID (`did:key:…`) as printed by `kotton org frost new`
* `--share <SHARE>` — Key share blob (hex) assigned to this participant by the initiator
* `--index <INDEX>` — Participant index assigned to this share (printed by the initiator)
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on behalf of



## `Kotton org frost sign-contribute`

Co-signer: contribute to an in-progress signing ceremony.

Run this on the co-signer's device.  The coordinator starts the ceremony with `kotton org grant issue --org <name>` and shares the session ID, message, and their commitment.  This command prints the arguments to paste back to the coordinator's `sign-finalize` command.

**Usage:** `Kotton org frost sign-contribute --org <ORG> --message-hex <MESSAGE_HEX> --coordinator-id <COORDINATOR_ID> --coordinator-commitment <COORDINATOR_COMMITMENT> --user <USER> <SESSION_ID>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<SESSION_ID>` — Session ID printed by `kotton org grant issue` on the coordinator

###### **Options:**

* `--org <ORG>` — Org DID (`did:key:…`)
* `--message-hex <MESSAGE_HEX>` — Message bytes to sign (hex), as printed by the coordinator
* `--coordinator-id <COORDINATOR_ID>` — Coordinator's FROST Identifier (hex), as printed by the coordinator
* `--coordinator-commitment <COORDINATOR_COMMITMENT>` — Coordinator's round-1 commitment (hex), as printed by the coordinator
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on behalf of



## `Kotton org frost sign-finalize`

Coordinator: finalize the signing ceremony and issue the GrantEnvelope.

Paste the three values printed by the co-signer's `sign-contribute` here.

**Usage:** `Kotton org frost sign-finalize --cosigner-id <COSIGNER_ID> --cosigner-commitment <COSIGNER_COMMITMENT> --cosigner-share <COSIGNER_SHARE> --user <USER> <SESSION_ID>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<SESSION_ID>` — Session ID from `kotton org grant issue`

###### **Options:**

* `--cosigner-id <COSIGNER_ID>` — Co-signer's FROST Identifier (hex), as printed by `sign-contribute`
* `--cosigner-commitment <COSIGNER_COMMITMENT>` — Co-signer's round-1 commitment (hex), as printed by `sign-contribute`
* `--cosigner-share <COSIGNER_SHARE>` — Co-signer's signature share (hex), as printed by `sign-contribute`
* `--user <USER>` — User ID to act on behalf of

## `Kotton model`

The models you have installed — add, ls, rm, use

**Usage:** `Kotton model <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `add` — Install a model from a weights file on this machine
* `ls` — List the installed models, and which one of each kind answers
* `rm` — Remove a model — its manifest and the weights it names
* `use` — Choose which model of its kind answers



## `Kotton model add`

Install a model from a weights file on this machine

**Usage:** `Kotton model add --manifest <MANIFEST> --user <USER> <FILE>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<FILE>` — The weights, as the publisher distributes them (`.gguf`, `.safetensors`)

###### **Options:**

* `--manifest <MANIFEST>` — A JSON `ModelManifest` describing those weights.

   Its fields are `name`, `version`, `weights` (the BLAKE3 hex of the file — `kotton model add` prints it if they disagree), `format` ("gguf" | "safetensors"), `kind` ("chat" | "embed" | "vision"), `parameters`, `quantisation`, `size`, `context_window`, `template`, and `licence` ({ "spdx", "text_hash" }). `publisher` is optional and is a display string — Kotton holds no key that says which models are real.
* `--user <USER>` — Identity to install into (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton model ls`

List the installed models, and which one of each kind answers

**Usage:** `Kotton model ls --user <USER>`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act on (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton model rm`

Remove a model — its manifest and the weights it names

**Usage:** `Kotton model rm --user <USER> <MODEL>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<MODEL>` — The model's name, its hash, or the first characters of its hash

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act on (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton model use`

Choose which model of its kind answers

**Usage:** `Kotton model use [OPTIONS] --user <USER> <MODEL>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<MODEL>` — The model's name, its hash, or the first characters of its hash

###### **Options:**

* `--rebuild-index` — Say yes to invalidating the index, which changing the active `embed` model does. Nothing else needs it: a chat model can be changed between two questions, and an embedding model cannot — every chunk the old one produced has to be built again, and two devices' indexes are only comparable while they name the same embedding model
* `--user <USER>` — Identity to act on (defaults to the active identity / KOTTON_USER)



## `Kotton net`

Network status snapshot (peers, gateways, sync, rendezvous)

**Usage:** `Kotton net [OPTIONS] --user <USER>`

###### **Options:**

* `--user <USER>` — User ID to authenticate as
* `--json` — Emit raw JSON instead of human-readable output (for scripting)
